Title: Anterior mediastinal nodular lesion segmentation from chest computed tomography imaging using UNet based neural network with attention mechanisms
Abstract: Automated detection of anterior mediastinal nodular lesions (AMLs) has significance for clinical usage as it is challenging for radiologists to accurately identify AMLs from chest computed tomography (CT) imaging due to various factors, including poor resolution, variations in intensity and the similarity of the AMLs to other tissues. To assist radiologists in AML detection from chest CT imaging, a UNet-based computer-aided detection (CADe) system is proposed to segment AMLs from slice images of the chest CT scans. The proposed network adopts a modified UNet architecture. To guide the proposed network to selectively focus on AMLs and potentially disregard others in the image, different attention mechanisms are utilized in the proposed network, including the self-attention mechanism and the convolutional block attention module (CBAM). The proposed network was trained and evaluated on 180 chest CT scans which consist of 180 AMLs. 90 AMLs were identified as thymic cysts, and 90 AMLs were diagnosed as thymoma. The proposed network achieved an average dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 93.23 with 5-fold cross-validation, for which the mean Intersection over Union (IoU), sensitivity and specificity were 90.29, 93.98 and 95.68 respectively. Our method demonstrated an improved segmentation performance over state-of-the-art segmentation networks, including UNet, ResUNet, TransUNet and UNet++. The proposed network employing attention mechanisms exhibited a promising result for segmenting AMLs from chest CT imaging and could be used to automate the AML detection process for achieving improved diagnostic reliability.

gold.abstract: To automatically detect Anterior Mediastinum Lesions (AMLs) in the Anterior Mediastinum (AM), the primary requirement will be an automatic segmentation model specifically designed for the AM. The prevalence of AML is extremely low, making it challenging to conduct screening research similar to lung cancer screening. Retrospectively reviewing chest CT scans over a specific period to investigate the prevalence of AML requires substantial time. Therefore, developing an Artificial Intelligence (AI) model to find location of AM helps radiologist to enhance their ability to manage workloads and improve diagnostic accuracy for AMLs. In this paper, we introduce a U-shaped structure network to segment AM. Two attention mechanisms were used for maintaining long-range dependencies and localization. In order to have the potential of Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and a lightweight network, we designed a parallel MHSA named Wide-MHSA (W-MHSA). Maintaining long-range dependencies is crucial for segmentation when we upsample feature maps. Therefore, we designed a Dilated Depth-Wise Parallel Path connection (DDWPP) for this purpose. In order to design a lightweight architecture, we introduced an expanding convolution block and combine it with the proposed W-MHSA for feature extraction in the encoder part of the proposed U-shaped network. The proposed network was trained on 2775 AM cases, which obtained an average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 87.83%, mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 79.16%, and Sensitivity of 89.60%. Our proposed architecture exhibited superior segmentation performance compared to the most advanced segmentation networks, such as Trans Unet, Attention Unet, Res Unet, and Res Unet++.

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper C provides an updated clinical guideline for lung cancer screening (LCS) using low-dose computed tomography (LDCT), with eligibility based on age (50–80), smoking history (≥20 pack-years, current or former), and exclusion of those with limited life expectancy. It emphasizes shared decision-making and smoking cessation counseling.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
- Paper C’s screening eligibility criteria can be operationalized as a risk-stratification rule. The proposal integrates this rule with a behavioral intervention framework (e.g., implementation intentions or default scheduling) to increase LCS uptake among eligible smokers. The causal link: guideline-based identification of high-risk individuals (Paper C) + a targeted behavioral nudge (from behavioral science) → higher screening completion rates and earlier detection.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Design: Two-arm randomized controlled trial in primary care clinics.
- Participants: Adults 50–80 with ≥20 pack-year smoking history, no lung cancer diagnosis, no life-limiting comorbidity (per Paper C).
- Intervention: Arm A receives standard shared decision-making plus a pre-scheduled LDCT appointment with opt-out framing and a mailed reminder. Arm B receives standard care (guideline-based discussion only).
- Measurements: Primary outcome = LDCT completion within 90 days. Secondary = smoking cessation referral uptake, stage at diagnosis (if any), and patient-reported decisional conflict.
- Validation: Use electronic health records to confirm eligibility and completion; compare baseline characteristics between arms.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project tests whether pairing the American Cancer Society’s 2023 lung cancer screening eligibility criteria with a behavioral scheduling intervention increases screening uptake among high-risk smokers. A randomized trial in primary care will compare standard shared decision-making to standard care plus pre-scheduled LDCT with opt-out framing. Outcomes include screening completion, cessation referral uptake, and stage at diagnosis. The contribution beyond Paper C is an actionable implementation strategy that converts guideline eligibility into actual screening behavior, addressing a known gap between recommendation and practice.

FINAL IDEA: Integrating the ACS lung cancer screening guideline with a behavioral scheduling intervention to test whether pre-scheduled opt-out LDCT appointments increase screening completion among guideline-eligible smokers.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper A (available) demonstrates that a specific neural network architecture improves prediction of protein–ligand binding affinity by encoding molecular graph topology. Paper B (available) shows that community-level social norms predict individual adherence to public-health guidelines, using longitudinal survey data and multilevel modeling.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Use the graph-topology encoding from Paper A to model the structure of social-contact networks that transmit norms. The causal link: network topology constrains norm diffusion, which (per Paper B) drives adherence. We hypothesize that topological features learned by the neural encoder (e.g., community boundaries, bridge nodes) predict adherence better than raw network density or individual-level attitudes.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Construct a contact-network dataset from mobile-phone proximity data in two regions. Extract graph embeddings using the Paper A architecture (retrained on network classification). Use embeddings as predictors in the multilevel model from Paper B, with adherence self-reports as outcome. Validate by comparing predictive accuracy against baseline network metrics (degree, clustering) and individual norm perception. Missing cross-paper knowledge: we do not know if the encoder generalizes from molecular graphs to social graphs; this must be tested via transfer learning.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
We propose a framework that transfers a graph-topology neural encoder from molecular affinity prediction to social-contact networks, then uses the learned embeddings as predictors of health-guideline adherence within a norm-diffusion multilevel model. The integration tests whether topology-derived latent features capture norm-transmission bottlenecks better than conventional network statistics. Expected contribution: a reusable bridge between geometric deep learning and social epidemiology, enabling topology-aware interventions.

FINAL IDEA: A graph-topology neural encoder from computational chemistry can be repurposed to extract latent features of social-contact networks that causally improve prediction of norm-driven health adherence in a multilevel model.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper C provides an updated clinical guideline for lung cancer screening (LCS) using low-dose computed tomography (LDCT), with eligibility based on age (50–80), smoking history (≥20 pack-years, current or former), and exclusion of those with limited life expectancy. It emphasizes shared decision-making and smoking cessation counseling.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
- Paper C’s screening eligibility criteria can be operationalized as a risk-stratification rule. The proposal integrates this rule with a behavioral intervention framework (e.g., implementation intentions or default scheduling) to increase LCS uptake among eligible smokers. The causal link: guideline-based identification of high-risk individuals (Paper C) + a targeted behavioral nudge (from behavioral science) → higher screening completion rates and earlier detection.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Design: Two-arm randomized controlled trial in primary care clinics.
- Participants: Adults 50–80 with ≥20 pack-year smoking history, no lung cancer diagnosis, no life-limiting comorbidity (per Paper C).
- Intervention: Arm A receives standard shared decision-making plus a pre-scheduled LDCT appointment with opt-out framing and a mailed reminder. Arm B receives standard care (guideline-based discussion only).
- Measurements: Primary outcome = LDCT completion within 90 days. Secondary = smoking cessation referral uptake, stage at diagnosis (if any), and patient-reported decisional conflict.
- Validation: Use electronic health records to confirm eligibility and completion; compare baseline characteristics between arms.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project tests whether pairing the American Cancer Society’s 2023 lung cancer screening eligibility criteria with a behavioral scheduling intervention increases screening uptake among high-risk smokers. A randomized trial in primary care will compare standard shared decision-making to standard care plus pre-scheduled LDCT with opt-out framing. Outcomes include screening completion, cessation referral uptake, and stage at diagnosis. The contribution beyond Paper C is an actionable implementation strategy that converts guideline eligibility into actual screening behavior, addressing a known gap between recommendation and practice.

FINAL IDEA: Integrating the ACS lung cancer screening guideline with a behavioral scheduling intervention to test whether pre-scheduled opt-out LDCT appointments increase screening completion among guideline-eligible smokers.

Causal/operational link: guideline-driven LDCT acquisition (Paper C) produces volumetric images that serve as input to Paper-b’s model, enabling opportunistic detection of anterior mediastinal lesions (AMLs) without additional radiation or separate visit.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Design: Prospective observational cohort nested within an existing LCS program. Enroll 500 consecutive guideline-eligible patients (per Paper C) undergoing baseline LDCT.
- Imaging: All LDCT scans (120 kVp, 40 mAs, 1.25 mm slice) are processed by Paper-b’s UNet+attention model, previously trained on diagnostic CT.
- Measurements: Model output = segmentation masks and classification (thymic cyst vs. thymoma) for any AML. Gold standard = two board-certified thoracic radiologists independently reviewing LDCT; discordance resolved by a third. Primary outcomes: sensitivity, specificity, DSC on LDCT; false-positive rate per 100 scans.
- Validation: External validation on a temporally separate cohort (next 200 patients) to avoid overfitting. Domain adaptation: fine-tune Paper-b on 50 LDCT scans with radiologist-annotated AMLs, then test on remaining 450; compare performance before/after fine-tuning.
- Missing knowledge: Paper-b’s training data were full-dose diagnostic CTs; LDCT has higher noise and different contrast. We explicitly test and report domain shift.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project integrates an attention-based UNet segmentation model for anterior mediastinal lesions with the ACS 2023 lung cancer screening guideline. By applying the model to LDCT scans from guideline-eligible smokers, we test whether automated detection of thymic cysts and thymoma can be achieved without additional imaging. The design includes prospective external validation, radiologist gold standard, and domain adaptation. The contribution beyond Paper-b is validation on low-dose screening CT; beyond Paper C is expansion of screening yield to mediastinal pathology.

FINAL IDEA: Applying a validated attention-UNet for anterior mediastinal lesion segmentation to LDCT scans from ACS guideline-eligible smokers to test opportunistic detection of thymic cysts and thymoma during lung cancer screening, with explicit domain adaptation and external validation.
transcript.C|1:
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper A (available) demonstrates that a specific neural network architecture improves prediction of protein–ligand binding affinity by encoding molecular graph topology. Paper B (available) shows that community-level social norms predict individual adherence to public-health guidelines, using longitudinal survey data and multilevel modeling.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Use the graph-topology encoding from Paper A to model the structure of social-contact networks that transmit norms. The causal link: network topology constrains norm diffusion, which (per Paper B) drives adherence. We hypothesize that topological features learned by the neural encoder (e.g., community boundaries, bridge nodes) predict adherence better than raw network density or individual-level attitudes.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Construct a contact-network dataset from mobile-phone proximity data in two regions. Extract graph embeddings using the Paper A architecture (retrained on network classification). Use embeddings as predictors in the multilevel model from Paper B, with adherence self-reports as outcome. Validate by comparing predictive accuracy against baseline network metrics (degree, clustering) and individual norm perception. Missing cross-paper knowledge: we do not know if the encoder generalizes from molecular graphs to social graphs; this must be tested via transfer learning.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
We propose a framework that transfers a graph-topology neural encoder from molecular affinity prediction to social-contact networks, then uses the learned embeddings as predictors of health-guideline adherence within a norm-diffusion multilevel model. The integration tests whether topology-derived latent features capture norm-transmission bottlenecks better than conventional network statistics. Expected contribution: a reusable bridge between geometric deep learning and social epidemiology, enabling topology-aware interventions.

FINAL IDEA: A graph-topology neural encoder from computational chemistry can be repurposed to extract latent features of social-contact networks that causally improve prediction of norm-driven health adherence in a multilevel model.
